d.title: The CPython pipeline
d.caption: Source text is tokenised, parsed into an AST, compiled to bytecode, and only then executed by the evaluation loop. Every performance, GIL and typing question in the course traces back to one of these five stages.

d.title: What happens on import
d.caption: The cache is keyed on the source's modification time and size; a stale or missing .pyc is recompiled transparently, which is why deleting __pycache__ is never a fix.

items.label: Look for __pycache__/mymod.cpython-312.pyc
items.desc: compare the header's mtime and size with the .py file

items.label: Cache hit → load the code object
items.desc: skips tokenising, parsing and compiling

items.label: Cache miss → compile and write the .pyc
items.desc: then execute the module body once

d.title: The implementations
d.caption: Same language, different runtimes. The standard library is shared; the execution engine and the extension-module story are not.

d.title: Where a virtual environment sits
d.caption: An environment is a directory with its own site-packages and a python that points at the base interpreter. Activating it only edits PATH; nothing is copied or compiled.

d.title: A variable is a name bound to an object
d.caption: After a = [1, 2, 3] and b = a there is one list and two names for it. Appending through either name changes the one object; rebinding b = [] only moves the name.

d.title: Arguments are passed by binding
d.caption: Calling f(a) binds the parameter name to the same object. Mutating it inside f is visible to the caller; assigning a new object to the parameter is not.

objects.note: a new object; the caller never sees it

d.title: 0.1 + 0.2 in binary
d.caption: A float is 53 significant bits; 0.1 is a repeating fraction in binary and is stored as 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827…, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False and money belongs in Decimal or integer cents.

d.title: bool is a subclass of int
d.caption: True and False are the integers 1 and 0 with a different __repr__. That is why True + True == 2, why sum(flags) counts, and why isinstance(True, int) is True.

d.title: str and bytes: encode one way, decode the other
d.caption: Text is a sequence of code points; bytes are a sequence of integers 0–255. The only bridge is an encoding, and UTF-8 is the one to name explicitly.

d.title: Indexing and slicing a string
d.caption: Positive indices count from 0 at the left; negative indices count from −1 at the right. s[1:4] takes indices 1, 2 and 3 — the stop is excluded.
d.label: s = 'Python'   s[1:4] == 'yth'   s[-1] == 'n'

d.title: What counts as false
d.caption: Everything else is truthy — including the strings '0' and 'False', an empty-looking object with no __bool__ or __len__, and any object you define yourself.

d.title: a < b < c is one expression
d.caption: Python evaluates b once and ands the two comparisons; it is not (a < b) < c. The chain can mix operators, which is where 0 < x == y reads as a trap.

d.title: Dynamic versus strong are different axes
d.caption: Python is dynamically typed (names carry no type) and strongly typed ('1' + 1 raises rather than guessing). JavaScript is dynamic and weak; C is static and weak; Rust is static and strong.

d.title: isinstance respects the hierarchy; type() does not
d.caption: type(True) is bool, so type(True) == int is False — but isinstance(True, int) is True because bool inherits from int. Prefer isinstance, and prefer duck typing to either.

d.title: Reading a traceback, bottom up
d.caption: The last line is the exception; the frame just above it is where it was raised; the frames above that are the callers. Read the bottom first, then walk up until you reach your own code.

items.label: Traceback (most recent call last):
items.desc: the header — frames follow, outermost first

items.label: File "app.py", line 12, in main
items.desc: your code: the caller

items.label: File "lib.py", line 40, in parse
items.desc: the callee, where it actually raised

items.label: ValueError: invalid literal for int()
items.desc: the exception type and message — read this first

d.title: A list is an array of references
d.caption: The list object holds a contiguous block of pointers to its elements plus a little spare capacity. Indexing is one pointer read — O(1); inserting at the front shifts every pointer — O(n).
d.label: len == 4, allocated 6: append is amortised O(1) because of the spare slots

d.title: Cost of the common list operations
d.caption: Green is O(1), amber O(n). The two that surprise people are 'in' and insert(0, x): both walk the whole list.

d.title: How a set finds an element
d.caption: hash(x) picks a slot; a collision probes onward. Membership is O(1) on average, which is why 'x in s' beats 'x in list' by orders of magnitude on large data — and why elements must be hashable.

d.title: Set algebra
d.caption: Each operator has a method form that accepts any iterable; the operator form needs sets on both sides. All four are O(len(a) + len(b)) and replace a nested loop.

d.title: How a dict finds a key
d.caption: Since 3.6 a dict is two arrays: a sparse index table and a dense array of entries in insertion order. Lookup hashes the key, finds the slot, and compares; iteration walks the dense array — which is why order is preserved.

d.title: Four ways to read a key
d.caption: Pick by what a missing key means: a bug (d[k]), a default (get), a default to store (setdefault), or something the structure should handle for you (defaultdict).

columns.title: d[k]
items: use when absence is a bug

d.title: Slice arithmetic
d.caption: seq[start:stop:step] takes start, start+step, … while below stop. seq[2:6] is indices 2, 3, 4, 5 — four items, which is stop − start. Negative indices count from the end; seq[::-1] reverses.
d.label: seq[2:6] → ['c','d','e','f']   seq[-3:] → ['f','g','h']   seq[::2] → ['a','c','e','g']

d.title: Shallow copy versus deep copy
d.caption: A shallow copy is a new outer list whose elements are the same inner objects; the nested lists are shared. copy.deepcopy copies recursively, so nothing is shared.

d.title: The mutable default is created once
d.caption: def f(items=[]) evaluates [] when def runs, and every call without an argument gets that same list. The fix is None as the default and a fresh list inside the body.

d.title: The four defences
d.caption: In order of preference: do not share, copy at the boundary, make it immutable, or document and own the sharing.

d.title: Nested conditions versus guard clauses
d.caption: Guard clauses handle the exceptional cases first and return; the happy path is left flat at the end, where it can be read in one pass.

d.title: What `for` actually does
d.caption: for calls iter() once, then next() until StopIteration. Any object with __iter__ can be looped over; the loop never uses indices unless you ask for them with enumerate.

d.title: break, continue and the loop else
d.caption: else runs only when the loop finished without break — the 'search failed' branch. continue jumps to the next iteration; pass does nothing at all.

nodes.label: else:
nodes.sub: ran to the end without break

d.title: Which structure, by the operation you need
d.caption: Choose by the operation that will run most often. Membership tests and key lookups want a hash table; ordered positional access wants a list; a fixed record wants a tuple.

d.title: Real data is nested
d.caption: An API response is dicts inside lists inside dicts. Each level is a separate object with its own lookup rules, and a missing key anywhere on the path raises unless you access it defensively.

d.title: zip stops at the shortest
d.caption: zip pairs items by position and stops when the shortest input is exhausted; the leftover 'd' is silently dropped. Pass strict=True (3.10+) to make a length mismatch an error.
d.label: zip(['a','b','c','d'], [1, 2, 3])

d.title: The four comprehension forms
d.caption: Same clause order in all four: expression, then for, then if. Brackets choose the result type; parentheses build a lazy generator that yields one item at a time.

columns.title: {k: v for k, v in ps}

d.title: def creates a function object and binds a name
d.caption: def runs like any other statement: it builds a function object (code, defaults, closure, docstring) and binds the name. That is why defaults are evaluated once, and why a function can be passed around like any value.

d.title: The six kinds of parameter, in the order they must appear
d.caption: Everything before / is positional-only; everything after * is keyword-only; *args and **kwargs collect whatever is left over. A signature is read left to right in exactly this order.
d.label: def f(a, /, b, *args, c, **kwargs)

d.title: LEGB: the four namespaces, searched inside out
d.caption: A name is looked up in the local scope, then any enclosing function scopes, then the module's globals, then the builtins. The first hit wins — which is how a local can shadow print().

d.title: A dispatch table replaces an if-chain
d.caption: Functions are values, so a dict from key to function is a switch that can be extended without editing the caller. handlers[kind](payload) does the routing.

d.title: map/filter versus a comprehension
d.caption: They are the same computation. The comprehension reads left to right and needs no lambda; map wins only when the function already exists and when laziness over a huge input matters.

columns.title: comprehension
items: [x for x in xs if x]

d.title: A closure keeps its enclosing variables alive
d.caption: make_counter returns inner, and inner holds a cell for count. The cell outlives make_counter's frame; each call to make_counter makes a new cell, so counters are independent.

d.title: The late-binding trap
d.caption: Lambdas in a loop close over the variable, not its value at that moment. All three see i's final value. The fix is a default argument, i=i, which captures the value at definition time.

items.label: fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
items.desc: three lambdas, all closing over the same i

items.label: the loop finishes with i == 2
items.desc: one variable, one final value

items.label: [f() for f in fns] → [2, 2, 2]
items.desc: each lambda reads i now, not then

items.label: lambda i=i: i  → [0, 1, 2]
items.desc: the default is evaluated at definition

d.title: @decorator is name rebinding
d.caption: @timed above def f is exactly f = timed(f). The decorator receives the function object, returns a wrapper, and the name f now points at the wrapper — the original survives only inside the wrapper's closure.

d.title: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up, run top-down
d.caption: @a above @b above def f is a(b(f)). b wraps f first, then a wraps that; on a call the outermost wrapper, a's, runs first.

items.label: @a  — applied last, runs first on a call
def f  — the original, runs last

d.title: Each recursive call adds a frame
d.caption: fact(4) pushes four frames before the base case returns; each frame holds its own n and its return address. Python caps the stack at about 1,000 frames, which is why deep recursion raises RecursionError and loops do not.

items.label: fact(1)  → returns 1
items.sub: base case — the top of the stack

d.title: Naive fib recomputes the same subproblems
d.caption: fib(5) calls fib(3) twice and fib(2) three times; the tree has about 1.6ⁿ nodes. Memoising with lru_cache makes each value computed once, turning exponential into linear.

d.title: Evolving a signature without breaking callers
d.caption: Add the new parameter as keyword-only with a default; deprecate the old one with a warning; remove it a release later. Callers that used keywords never notice.

items.label: def send(msg, *, retries=3)
items.desc: new parameter, keyword-only, defaulted

items.label: accept the old name, warn
items.desc: warnings.warn('use retries=', DeprecationWarning)

items.label: remove the old name next release
items.desc: the warning gave callers a version to migrate in

d.title: What happens when you call a class
d.caption: Point(1, 2) is type.__call__: allocate with __new__, initialise with __init__, return the instance. __init__ never returns the object — it configures one that already exists.

items.label: Point(1, 2)
items.desc: the class is callable because its metaclass defines __call__

items.label: obj = Point.__new__(Point, 1, 2)
items.desc: allocate a bare instance — rarely overridden

items.label: obj.__init__(1, 2)
items.desc: set attributes on the new instance; returns None

items.label: return obj
items.desc: the caller gets the initialised instance

d.title: Attribute lookup on an instance
d.caption: obj.x checks data descriptors on the type, then the instance __dict__, then the class and its MRO. Assignment always writes to the instance __dict__ — which is how an instance attribute shadows a class attribute.

items.label: data descriptor on type(obj)?
items.desc: property, slots — wins over the instance

items.label: obj.__dict__['x']?
items.desc: the instance's own attributes

items.label: class attribute along the MRO?
items.desc: methods live here; non-data descriptors bind

items.label: __getattr__, else AttributeError
items.desc: the last resort

d.title: Three kinds of method, one difference
d.caption: The decorator decides what arrives as the first argument: the instance, the class, or nothing. Everything else about them is the same function machinery.

columns.title: @staticmethod
items: usually a module function in disguise

d.title: A property looks like an attribute and runs code
d.caption: obj.area reads like a field; behind it a getter runs. Start with a plain attribute, and add a property only when reading or writing needs logic — callers never change.

nodes.label: @property area
nodes.sub: a data descriptor on the class

d.title: The diamond, linearised by C3
d.caption: class D(B, C) with both B and C deriving from A gives the MRO D → B → C → A → object. Each class appears once, parents come after children, and the order of the bases is respected — which is what makes super() cooperative.

children.label: D(B, C)
children.sub: MRO: D, B, C, A, object

d.title: Duck typing, protocols and ABCs
d.caption: Three ways to say 'anything that behaves like X'. Duck typing checks nothing; a Protocol lets the type checker verify structure; an ABC verifies at runtime by inheritance or registration.

d.title: The class explosion
d.caption: Every combination of two axes needs its own subclass: 2 × 3 today, 3 × 4 next quarter. Composition holds one object per axis and combines them at runtime.

d.title: Composition: has-a instead of is-a
d.caption: Report holds a renderer and a data source; new combinations are constructor arguments, not new classes.

d.title: Template method: the ABC owns the skeleton
d.caption: run() in the base class fixes the order of steps; subclasses fill in the abstract ones. The base never needs to know which subclass it is.

d.title: __eq__ and __hash__ are one decision
d.caption: Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes the class unhashable. Equal objects must hash equal, so hash the same fields you compare — and only if they are immutable.
rows: define both on the same fields

d.title: What @dataclass generates
d.caption: From the annotated fields it writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ (and __hash__, ordering and __slots__ on request). The class body stays a declaration of fields.

d.title: Dataclass, NamedTuple or Pydantic
d.caption: Choose by what the object is for: a mutable record, an immutable lightweight tuple, or validated data crossing a boundary.

d.title: SOLID in Python
d.caption: Two principles survive intact, one matters most, and two mostly dissolve because Python has first-class functions and duck typing.

columns.title: Weakens
items: O — extension via composition, not subclassing

columns.title: Dissolves
items: I — duck typing segregates for free
D — pass a function or an object

d.title: Observer, in Python
d.caption: Subscribers are just callables in a list. Publishing is a loop; no Observer interface, no abstract update method.

d.title: State: the transitions are the design
d.caption: An order moves through states along allowed edges only; the state machine is a dict of transitions and a check, not a class per state.
